In brief In a 2004 war model by Alastair Smith and me, two sides who disagree learn from each battle, and I show that its rule for accepting offers fails in its own example. Then each side gets its own cost per battle, so that one side, which I call the machine, can fight for free. I prove that for the model’s kind of beliefs and a prize worth something, settlement still comes by a finite deadline, unless the war is decided first, whenever the humans pay anything per battle. I compute specific settlement chances and shares for one main setup, which I call the baseline, and for variations on it. In runs with a free machine and a human cost of 0.5, when the machine wins 80 to 99 percent of battles and its starting estimate of its own chance of winning a battle is below the true chance, wars usually end in human surrender or outright machine victory, except when beliefs start close together or at 80 percent with human offers in the baseline.

Part 1. I check what my older war models prove, then let one side fight for free

I wrote this work as part of a series. Two other papers of the series, The War Baseline and Disagreement Without Hidden Information, my papers on the commitment problem in power transitions and on differing beliefs in the AI transition, lean on four works I wrote with colleagues: Smith and Stam (2001), Smith and Stam (2004), Bennett, Smith and Stam (2003), and Friedman, Wittman and Stam (2003). The second also cites an earlier draft by Alastair Smith (Smith 1998b) for a result on superweapons.

Here I ask five questions about those models and the way the series uses them:

  1. Of the results those two papers lean on, which are proved, and which are arguments or worked examples?
  2. In the 2004 bargaining model by Smith and me, is the published rule for the side receiving an offer that side’s best choice?
  3. Do the numbers printed in that article follow from the definitions in its own text?
  4. If a machine pays nothing to fight and humans pay something per battle, does learning from battles still end the war by a finite date? On what terms?
  5. How much of that answer is proved in general, and how much is computed for one set of numbers?

The short answers: a correction, a mismatch, and a deadline that survives

First, most of what the earlier works supply is argued in prose or shown by worked example, not proved. Every one of their main models, and every war they compute, gives both sides the same cost of fighting. One of them, by Friedman, Wittman and me, extends its one-round argument to unequal costs.

Second, the 2004 article’s rule for the side answering an offer is not that side’s best choice in the article’s own running example. The rule says to accept any offer worth at least what fighting to the very end would bring. But an offer can never be less than zero. So turning an offer down lets that side accept zero, or something better, later on, instead of fighting to the finish at a loss. The corrected rule accepts an offer only when it is worth at least as much as turning it down.

Third, when I compute the 2004 example from the definitions in the article’s text, two of its printed figures do not come out. Two departures from those definitions reproduce every transcribed number in both figures. That does not show how the published numbers were first produced.

Fourth, in my extended model a deadline survives. The side making the offers bears both sides’ costs of delay. So for the kind of beliefs the model uses, and a prize worth something, every pattern of best play settles by a finite deadline whenever the two costs add up to more than zero, unless the war is decided first. A positive human cost is enough, even when the machine’s cost is zero. Fighting for free delays settlement by learning. It does not abolish it.

Fifth, the deadline’s bound and several other results are proved and checked by a proof-checking program called Lean 4. Such a program confirms that each conclusion follows from the stated assumptions, not that the assumptions hold in the world. The specific deadlines, chances and shares are computed, for one baseline and variations on it.

Costs of fighting matter as much as the stakes

The cost of fighting decides a great deal in these models. In the 2001 models, as Smith and I wrote, “If the cost of fighting is zero, then generically nations fight in every state,” and “As fighting becomes extremely costly, war never occurs” (Smith and Stam 2001). High costs allow several possible patterns of best play, as in a game of chicken, so which peace holds depends on coordination. Low costs can also deter, because “nations are reluctant to surrender when attacked” (Smith and Stam 2001).

Yet every computed war in those works gives both sides the same cost per battle. None of the models I draw on in which the sides learn about battle strength as they fight has one side that both wins most battles and fights for free. So I build one.

The extension gives each side its own cost per battle and solves the 2004 model for best play under the corrected rule. I use “machine” and “humans” only to name the two sides, each of which can have a cost of zero or more per battle. The labels carry nothing else. My contribution is the correction of the 2004 rule and this extension to unequal costs. The other two papers of the series draw on its results.

Part 2. Most of what my earlier models supply is argued or shown by example, with both sides paying the same cost

This part sets out what four of the earlier works assume and what each actually proves. Part 3 turns to the 2004 article. In every one of the four, both sides pay the same cost of fighting in the main model. Friedman, Wittman and I extend our argument to unequal costs, but only for a single round. These four are unpublished drafts, available only from me on request, so this audit can be checked only on request.

The 2001 model argues, without proof, that no deal holds when sides fight over forts

Think of a marker on a tug-of-war rope. (This is an analogy for the model’s set-up.) Each round the marker moves one notch toward one side, one notch toward the other, or stays put, by chance. The game ends when it reaches either end.

In Smith and Stam (2001), “Issues, Stakes and the Nature of War,” the notches are states numbered from zero up to the number of forts. Each state is read as the number of forts nation A holds. Reaching either end is decisive defeat for one side and victory for the other; as the paper notes, “this model is called a random walk or a gambler’s ruin.” Each round A takes a fort, B takes one, or neither does (Figure 1, panel a).

Each nation chooses whether to attack, resist or surrender. Both pay the same cost for each battle, and later payoffs count for less than earlier ones. Plans may look only at the current state, and they switch at fixed cut points. Under best play, the states fall into as many as five zones in a row: one side capitulates, war, a peaceful status quo, war, and the other side capitulates (Figure 1, panel b). As the paper puts it, “[f]or some parameter values, some of these zones collapse to zero length.”

The paper compares three things to fight over:

  • in the forts model, nations value the forts they hold, and the chance of winning a battle does not change with the state;
  • in the power model, holding more forts raises a side’s chance of winning the next battle, by an amount set by how decisive battles are;
  • in the policy model, nations fight over a policy, and a decisive winner imposes its own preferred policy in place of the status quo.

In the power model, nations value the forts they hold. In the policy model, the possible policies are represented on a scale from zero to one.

The conference paper states no proposition, lemma or theorem. It credits two results to Smith (1997, 1998a): a best answer to a cut-point plan is itself a cut-point plan, and best play among such plans exists when nations can randomize at the cut points. In its own text it derives only the two cost limits quoted in Part 1.

The claim most used in The War Baseline is that “No agreements can be reached in the forts or the power models” (Smith and Stam 2001). The paper argues it case by case, not by proof. Whichever side would gain from a deal cannot credibly promise not to attack once the balance of forts moves its way. The argument relies on each shift in the balance making continued play strictly more valuable to the side that gains a fort and less valuable to the other. A footnote concedes that one step in that argument can fail at certain cut points.

Two other claims rest only on numerical examples. One is that deals that enforce themselves are sometimes possible in the policy model. The other is that nations surrender fastest in the power model, where the status-quo zone is smaller. A credible exit bought “with money, or some other transferable utility” is stated in prose only.

Smith’s 1998 draft uses one example to argue that a winning side is likelier to use a superweapon

Disagreement Without Hidden Information also cites a draft by Smith dated 26 February 1998, which calls itself “extremely preliminary and in parts incomplete” (Smith 1998b). It uses the same random walk and shared battle cost as the 2001 paper and states no proposition. It treats superweapons in a single numerical example. In its words, superweapons “have three characteristics: the initial advantage they confer, the length of time before the enemy can replicate them, and how they affect the costs of fighting” (Smith 1998b).

In the example, an unannounced weapon captures forts on its first use, is copied within one period, and then raises both sides’ cost of fighting. Smith warns that the example “was generated using a different stage game to that considered in the rest of the paper” (Smith 1998b). In that game nations choose only between fighting and surrender. Higher costs push a losing side toward surrender. So the draft concludes from the example that nations are most likely to use a superweapon “when they are winning the war rather than as a last ditch gamble for resurrection” (Smith 1998b).

The 2003 spiral paper shows by example only that shared news can feed both sides’ optimism

Bennett, Smith and Stam (2003), “Spirals of Optimism and the Nature of War,” joins a model of beliefs that drift apart before a war to the bargaining game of the 2004 article. As we wrote, “In our model, what is spiraling is the two sides’ optimism about their chances of victory in some future war” (Bennett, Smith and Stam 2003).

The pattern behind it is a finding by Bennett and me that an arms race roughly doubles the risk of war (Bennett and Stam 2004). The model takes this as its premise and does not test it. The doubling is printed without a margin of error. The underlying estimate’s 95 percent interval, once converted, runs from about 1 to about 4, so it includes 1, which would mean no effect. The War Baseline discusses this.

The paper’s formal results on bargaining are the 2004 article’s, word for word. Its own contribution, the spiral of optimism, carries no proposition. It uses a simulation example, the same one later printed in the 2004 article. In it, two nations with different theories of what wins wars watch the same war between others and both grow optimistic. When the two fight a war between them and only the factor both sides believe in is present, their computed expectations of winning the next battle add up to 0.97. That is joint pessimism about the next battle.

Of technological change keeping beliefs apart, the paper says “we demonstrate this formally” (Bennett, Smith and Stam 2003). What follows is only a statement. If a factor’s weight drifts by independent random steps and no new information arrives, the spread of beliefs about that weight grows with time.

Sealed offers in one round: proved for the basic game, argued for unequal costs

Friedman, Wittman and Stam (2003), “International Politics with Symmetric Bargaining and Two-Sided Incomplete Information,” studies a single round of bargaining. It keeps the courtroom terms of the model it grew from. An aggressor and a target each privately see an independent signal of how a war would turn out. At the same moment they submit a demand and an offer “to a third party (perhaps a computer). If the offer is greater than or equal to the demand, then there is a settlement half way between the two; otherwise, the case proceeds to war” (Friedman, Wittman and Stam 2003). In war, the outcome is the average of the two signals, and each side pays the same cost.

The paper proves a lemma and six propositions exactly for the basic game, in which signals are spread evenly over a scale from zero to one. They give the best plans for demands and offers, which are made up of straight-line pieces in each side’s signal. They show that every non-trivial symmetric pattern of best play of that kind leads to the same outcome. They give the exact chance of war at each common cost, and how the chance and outcomes of war move with the cost and the spread of signals. We defended the single round as “an upper bound on bargaining efficiency” (Friedman, Wittman and Stam 2003).

Extensions to other kinds of signals, unequal splits and unequal costs are argued, not proved. Friedman, Wittman and I concluded that “our main qualitative results appear to be quite robust.” For unequal costs, the paper argues as follows for the basic game, over the relevant range. One more unit of cost for the target alone raises the target’s offer by one and a half units and lowers the aggressor’s demand by half a unit. So for equal shifts in both sides’ costs, “75% of the impact is due to own cost and 25% to the other player’s cost” (Friedman, Wittman and Stam 2003). That is a result about offers in one round. It says nothing about how long a war lasts or when fighting stops.

Part 3. In the 2004 model, two sides who disagree, with nothing hidden, learn from every battle

From Part 4 on, I correct and extend the model of “Bargaining and the Nature of War” (Smith and Stam 2004). Two nations, A and B, dispute a prize worth more than zero. As in the 2001 model, war is a random walk along a line of forts, and reaching either end is decisive. But here the chance that A wins a battle is fixed, wherever the front stands.

Each period, before any fighting, A makes a take-it-or-leave-it offer to divide the prize (Figure 2, panel a). If B accepts, the game ends on those terms. If B refuses, they fight one battle. The winner takes a fort from the loser, both pay the same cost per battle, and later payoffs are not discounted.

The central change is in belief. The two sides start with different beliefs about A’s chance of winning a battle. Each side knows the other’s starting belief, neither holds private information, and after every battle each updates its own belief by the standard rule of probability (Bayes’ rule). The starting beliefs are public, so each side also knows that the other knows both beliefs. In the article’s examples, each belief takes a standard form set by two numbers (a beta distribution). “To our knowledge,” we wrote, “within the political science literature, our model is the first game-theoretic model to dispense with the common-priors assumption” (Smith and Stam 2004).

A web appendix examines a version in which the sides take turns making offers. In the article’s words, it “produces similar results to the one-sided bargaining used here” (Smith and Stam 2004). The web appendix works out that version without reporting a numerical comparison.

The article proves four of its five formal results

One term recurs from here on. A side’s value of fighting to the end is what it expects to get if no deal is ever struck and the two fight until one holds every fort. The 2004 article states five formal results and proves four of them:

  • Proposition 1 gives a condition any settlement needs. War goes on whenever the two sides’ values of fighting to the end add up to more than the prize. As Smith and I noted, this holds under any bargaining rule in which a settlement needs both sides’ consent.
  • Lemma 1 says the two sides’ beliefs come together as battles pile up.
  • Proposition 2 says that after some finite date, A offers B the larger of zero and B’s value of fighting to the end, and B accepts. So the war ends in finite time, by decisive defeat or by a settlement.
  • A Corollary, stated without proof, says that the cheaper each battle, the later that date.
  • Proposition 3 gives A’s values by working back from the end under Proposition 2’s offer rule.

Everything else in the article rests on worked examples

The article’s running example has ten forts, a start in the middle at state 5, a prize of 30, and a shared cost of 1 per battle. A’s starting belief is set by the numbers four and two, and B’s by two and four. In plain terms, A expects to win two battles in three, and B expects A to win one in three. The article leaves the true chance unspecified.

At the start, computed from the text’s definitions, each side’s value of fighting to the end is 10.15. The article reports that A values fighting the next battle at 23.8 and settling at 17.8, so A fights. Its printed Figure 3 gives 23.76 and 17.78, which implies 12.22 for B’s value of fighting to the end. The article also reports that by period 10, settling and fighting are worth the same to A in every state.

The article’s account of why beliefs drift apart before a war carries no proposition. Like the spiral paper, it uses a three-factor example in which both sides watch a third country win five straight battles. They update by simulation, because exact beliefs are “often analytically intractable” (Smith and Stam 2004). Technological change enters as a drift in the factors’ weights. Its only formal content is that the spread of beliefs grows with time.

The article’s claims about how long a peace lasts after a war rest on one numerical comparison. After an early settlement at state 7 in period 2, A puts its chance of winning a battle at three in four, and B puts it at one in two. A shock worth one battle won by B then moves B’s estimate of A’s chance to four in nine. After a ten-period war ending at state 5, their estimates of A’s chance are nine in sixteen and seven in sixteen, and the same shock moves B’s estimate to seven in seventeen, “a shift of less than half the magnitude” (Smith and Stam 2004).

Part 4. The 2004 rule for answering an offer is not a best choice, and the printed tables do not follow from the text

In setting up its solution, the 2004 article has B accept any offer at least equal to B’s value of fighting to the end. I call this the published rule. In the article’s own running example, it is not B’s best response.

Refusing an offer keeps the chance of a better one

Think of selling a used car. (An analogy, not part of the model.) A buyer offers less than you expect another buyer to offer next week. Keeping the car another week costs you something. But if the better offer is likely enough, saying no is right. You weigh today’s offer against next week’s offer, not against scrapping the car.

The model works the same way. Offers cannot be negative: the least A can offer B is zero. When B refuses and fights one more battle, B is not committed to fighting to the end at a loss. Next period B again faces an offer of at least zero. It may even face a positive offer, if the battle moves the war to a state where A prefers to settle.

So what B gives up by accepting is not its value of fighting to the end. It is its value of refusing: one battle’s cost set against what B expects to get a period later (in the technical paper I call this the “value of rejecting”). The article’s proof of Proposition 2 applies the zero floor at the current state. It ignores the floor, and the positive offers, at later states.

I prove that the published rule therefore fails at a settlement state whenever both of these hold:

  • B’s value of fighting to the end is zero or more there; and
  • it is below zero at some later settlement state that the war can reach through fighting.

Where that value is already below zero at the current state, the test is B’s value of refusing against A’s whole plan.

On the article’s own printed Figure 3, refusing beats the offer

One can check this on the article’s printed Figure 3 without solving the model again (Figure 3, panel a). From the start at state 5, five battles through states that the printed figure marks as fighting can take the war to state 6 in period 5. There B’s value of fighting to the end is below zero. The printed table has A settle by offering B nothing.

Suppose B refuses. It pays the one-battle cost of 1. By B’s updated belief, A wins the next battle with chance 5 in 11, moving the war to state 7, where B again gets nothing. B wins with chance 6 in 11, moving the war to state 5 in period 6. There the printed figure has A settle and leave B 30 minus 25.73, which is 4.27. So refusing is worth about 1.33 to B, which is more than the nothing it was offered.

This is a deduction from the printed cells. It is proved and checked by the program, given the cells as transcribed. Refusing still beats accepting zero after allowing for the rounding of the printed numbers. It also beats accepting zero whenever B puts A’s chance of winning the next battle below 327 in 427.

Computed from the text, the rule fails on the path of play and at every late date

Computed exactly from the definitions in the article’s text, the published rule fails right on the path of play from the start. At state 6 in period 1, refusing once and then following the published play is worth 3.10 to B. The published offer is 1.73, and the best plan after refusing is worth 4.58. Refusing once pays strictly at four more states along that path through period 8. The best plan after refusing favours refusal at nine states on the path in all. These failures are computed.

The rule also fails at every late date that battles can still reach: at state 3 on even dates and at state 4 on odd ones. There B’s value of refusing under best play is more than the published offer, and every pattern of best play refuses it. This is proved and checked by the program.

The corrected rule: accept an offer only if refusing is worth no more

Both starting beliefs are known and every battle is public, so the 2004 game hides nothing; only chance is uncertain. Under the corrected rule, B accepts an offer worth more than refusing and refuses one worth less. What B expects to get at any state is the larger of zero and its value of refusing there. That is never below its value of fighting to the end.

Exact ties need rules of their own. At an exact match, B must accept if A strictly prefers to settle and could offer more, since otherwise A would have no best offer. Accepting at the other exact matches, and settling when A is exactly indifferent, are tie rules I select.

Most of the 2004 results survive, two of them in amended form

With the rule corrected, the article’s formal results stand as follows. I prove each of them.

  • Proposition 1 holds as printed, as a condition any settlement needs. Under best play it sharpens: settling requires A’s value of fighting to the end to be at most the prize minus the offer A would make to B under best play.
  • Lemma 1 holds. Once the number of battles reaches or exceeds the number of forts, at every undecided state the war can reach, each side’s total wins are at least half the difference between the number of battles and the number of forts. For two-number beliefs of the kind the examples use, the two sides’ beliefs converge, evenly across those states. As battles pile up, the two sides assign nearly the same probability to any set of possible battle odds, with the same bound on the difference across all those sets and states. At every such state, both beliefs crowd toward one half, whatever the true chance. So the sides come to agree near even odds, which is right only when the true odds are even.
  • Propositions 2 and 3 hold once B’s value of fighting to the end is replaced by its value of refusing. For those two-number beliefs, when the costs add up to more than zero, there is a finite date from which A offers B the larger of zero and B’s value of refusing, and B accepts. This holds in every pattern of best play and at every state the war can reach. In the baseline at a cost of 1, that proved date is period 25 at the latest. A’s values then follow the article’s working-back recursion (a step-by-step rule that defines each period’s values from the next period’s) against that offer.

Three terms carry fixed meanings from here on, including the last battle and the deadline

To compare when settlement comes, I fix three terms.

  • A state the war can reach in a period is an undecided state that some run of that many battles leads to without first hitting either end. It counts whether or not a settlement would have ended the war along the way.
  • The last battle is the last period in which some state the war can reach still fights.
  • The deadline is the first period from which every state the war can reach settles. It is always the last battle plus one.

Because the deadline counts states that actual play may never visit, it is an outer bound. It is not the time at which wars actually settle.

Rebuilt from its text, the 2004 model keeps its shape but not its printed numbers

When I rebuild the baseline from the definitions in the article’s text, some numbers match to the last printed digit. These are B’s average beliefs after the first battle (two in seven after a B win and three in seven after an A win) and the web appendix’s shares under turn-taking. Best play keeps the shape shown in Figure 2. But the article’s printed Figures 1 and 3 do not follow from the text’s definitions:

  • In printed Figure 1, the chances of eventual victory differ from mine by up to 0.025, and the expected lengths of war by up to 10.3 periods.
  • At the start, each side’s value of fighting to the end is 10.15, and A’s value of fighting the next battle is 23.76, which matches the printed 23.8. But A’s value of settling under the published rule is 30 minus 10.15, or 19.85, not the printed 17.8.
  • In printed Figure 3, values differ by up to 9.68. Under the published rule, the last battle and deadline fall in periods 7 and 8, not the printed 9 and 10.

Under the corrected rule, computed from the text’s definitions, the baseline’s last battle falls in period 5 and its deadline in period 6 (Figure 3, panel b). At even battle odds, B’s expected share of the prize of 30, given a settlement, rises from 6.30 to 8.83. Settlement before a decisive victory stays certain.

As the shared cost per battle falls from 1 to 0.5, 0.25, 0.1 and 0.05, the computed deadline under the corrected rule lengthens from 6 periods to 12, 25, 61 and 121. These computed choices are certified. To certify the choices, a second calculation starts beyond the date by which best play is proved to settle everywhere and checks the choices against explicit bounds on error from the cut-off and from arithmetic.

So how were the printed numbers produced? I do not establish it. One computation reproduces them. It makes two departures from the text’s definitions. It measures B’s expected length of war from the starting state, 5, in every cell, rather than from that cell’s own state. And it lowers each of a belief’s two numbers by one half in the two integrals—the formulas that average eventual victory chances and war lengths over a side’s belief. With both departures, the 15 supplied cells (each printing a pair of numbers) in printed Figure 1 and all 42 printed cells of printed Figure 3 come out to their printed rounding, in every number and every choice to fight or settle. So do the printed last battle and deadline, 9 and 10, when settlement is imposed at period 10. Solved from a longer horizon, the same computation gives 11 and 12. The same departures also reproduce the 0.62 chance of victory and the 15.46 expected length of war quoted by Bennett, Smith and Stam (2003), where the text’s definitions give 0.600 and 16.27. None of this shows how the article’s own figures were computed, and this computation carries no certificate. My extension follows the definitions in the text.

Part 5. In my model, a machine that fights for free still faces a deadline

None of the earlier learning models I draw on has a strong side that fights for free

In the main models and every computed war so far, both sides pay the same cost per battle. The only analysis of unequal costs is the one-round result of Friedman, Wittman and me. The 2004 article cites a 2005 chapter by Smith and me on disagreement over costs. A footnote in Smith and Stam (2003) sketches costs learned through battle.

In that 2005 chapter, which I read from its page proofs, the battle odds are fixed and not in dispute. Side A pays a known cost. That cost stays the same from battle to battle. Side B’s cost is either low or high, one unit apart. The two sides hold different beliefs about how likely the high cost is, and they update those beliefs as battles reveal it, under the 2004 rule. Their starting beliefs use the same two-number form as in the 2004 article, and the updates use the count of high-cost battles. In the worked example, the side that pays almost nothing per battle, 0.01, is the side certain to lose every battle.

My extension differs in four ways:

  • both costs are known numbers;
  • the sides disagree, and learn, about the battle odds, not about a cost;
  • the side that fights for free wins half its battles in the baseline, and 80 to 99 percent in the high-odds runs, whereas in the 2005 example the near-free side wins none;
  • the game is solved under the corrected rule.

In my model the machine takes A’s place and the humans take B’s. The baseline copies the 2004 running example. It has ten forts, a start at state 5, and a prize of 30. The machine’s starting belief is set by four and two, and the humans’ by two and four.

Best play exists, and its values are unique when the prize is worth something

Under the corrected rule, I prove that for every pair of costs there is at least one plan that prescribes best play after every possible history. Game theorists call such a plan a subgame-perfect equilibrium. In it, each side acts on its own stopping value. For the answering side, that is the larger of zero and its value of refusing; for the offering side, it is the value worked back against that offer. A side making the offers settles when it is exactly indifferent.

I also prove when best play is unique in what matters. This holds when the prize is worth something, or when the machine’s cost is zero and the machine makes the offers. Then every pattern of best play gives both sides the same values at every state and the same offer at every settlement. It also gives the same choice to settle or fight, wherever the side making the offer is not exactly indifferent. Patterns can differ only in choices that change no value, such as which losing offer a side makes when it means to fight anyway.

Without a settlement, the war still ends. A random walk along a finite line of forts reaches one end in finite expected time.

The side making the offers pays for both sides’ delay, so the humans’ cost alone forces a deadline

Go back to the used car, now from the buyer’s side. (Again an analogy only.) If the seller turns down today’s offer, they must pay to keep the car another week, so today they will take a little less than they expect next week. A buyer who waits a week loses that discount and pays their own costs of waiting too.

The model works the same way. Whichever side makes the take-it-or-leave-it offer takes all the surplus above what refusing is worth to the other side. A side that puts off settling by one battle pays its own battle cost directly. It also pays the other side’s battle cost indirectly, through the higher offer the other side will demand tomorrow.

I prove this precisely, for either side making the offers, under the corrected rule. It holds at any state where the answering side’s value of refusing is zero or more. There the offering side prefers settling now to fighting one battle and settling next period exactly when its gain from waiting is at most the two costs added together. That gain (the technical paper’s “leverage gain”) is the answering side’s expectation of its own value one battle on minus the offering side’s expectation of that value.

Learning shrinks that gain. As battles pile up, the two sides’ beliefs come together. Suppose the gap between the two sides’ estimates of the machine’s chance of winning the next battle falls below the sum of the two costs divided by the prize, at every state the war can reach. Then one more battle can no longer gain the offering side as much as it costs the two sides combined (Figure 4, panel a).

So I prove the following, for the model’s kind of beliefs, a prize worth something, and costs that add up to more than zero. There is a finite date from which every pattern of best play settles at every state the war can reach, whatever the machine’s cost. The bound on that date grows in proportion to the prize divided by the sum of the costs, and it depends only on that ratio and the starting beliefs. So a positive human cost keeps the deadline finite even when the machine fights completely for free, whichever side makes the offers.

In the baseline, the gap between the two sides’ estimates of the machine’s chance of winning the next battle starts at one third. It shrinks in the same way at every state the war can reach. With equal costs of 1, it reaches the threshold in period 24, which is the proved bound for the plan I compute. The bound for every pattern of best play is one period later, period 25. The computed deadline is period 6.

The deadline also has a floor, so it recedes without limit only as both costs vanish

For the baseline beliefs with the machine making the offers, the deadline also has a proved lower bound. That bound also grows as the sum of the costs shrinks. The formal files prove this for costs below a threshold. They show the threshold exists but do not state it.

A separate one-step test gives concrete floors. It is proved on paper, not checked by the program. With a free machine and a human cost of 0.1, the last battle comes no earlier than period 80. With equal costs of 0.02, it comes no earlier than period 278. The matching upper bounds on the deadline are 594 and 1,494 for the plan I compute, and 595 and 1,495 for every pattern of best play. So the deadline recedes without limit only when both costs fall to zero together.

Raising the machine’s cost works the other way. I prove that as it rises, the set of states where the machine strictly prefers to fight shrinks. The last battle and the deadline of the plan I compute never move later, whenever they are finite.

Computed deadlines fall inside the proved bounds and move with them

The computed deadlines in the baseline, with certified decisions, fall inside the proved bounds and move with them (Figure 4, panel b). Here is what happens when the machine’s cost drops from the humans’ level to zero:

  • humans’ cost 1: the deadline moves from period 6 to period 18 when the machine makes the offers, and to period 12 when the humans do;
  • humans’ cost 0.5: from 12 to 32 with machine offers, or to 25 with human offers;
  • humans’ cost 0.2: from 31 to 68, or to 63.

A far-off deadline does not mean settlement comes. In the baseline at even battle odds, with equal costs of 0.02, the computed chance that a decisive victory comes first rounds to 1.000.

If the machine is in fact far stronger, winning 80 to 99 percent of battles, the deadline does not change at all, because plans depend only on the two sides’ beliefs. But in those runs, with a free machine and a human cost of 0.5, the war ends in about 3 to 8 battles on average, long before the deadline (Part 8).

Part 6. In my baseline with a free machine at even odds, more than half of wars settle once the humans’ cost passes a point between 0.35 and 0.40

A range of deals both sides prefer to fighting to the end is needed, but not enough

Costs enter a second time, in the range of divisions that both sides prefer to fighting to the finish. Call the two sides’ joint optimism the prize times the amount by which their own expected chances of winning the war add up to more than one. I prove that, with unequal costs, Proposition 1 becomes this condition. Such a division exists only if the joint optimism is no more than two amounts added together: the machine’s cost per battle times its expected battles left, and the humans’ cost per battle times theirs. When the two expected costs together cover the joint optimism, there is at least one division both sides would take over fighting to the end. With a free machine, only the humans’ part remains.

This condition defines what I call the simple bargaining range (the technical paper’s “static benchmark”). In the baseline with a free machine, the range is empty at the start of the war for any human cost below 1.29 of 30 per battle, about 4.3 percent of the prize. I prove that it opens later, as battles bring beliefs together, whenever the humans’ cost is above zero.

Even when it is open, the range is a condition a deal needs, not a guarantee of one. In the 2004 baseline at equal costs of 1, a range of 9.70 is already open at the start. Yet the machine still fights in period 0, because waiting for battles to shift beliefs promises more than settling now. Nor is the range the set of offers accepted under best play. There the answering side refuses anything below its true value of refusing.

The humans’ value has a proved floor and ceiling when the machine makes the offers

In every pattern of best play with the machine making the offers, I prove three things about the humans’ expected value, judged by their own beliefs:

  • it is at least zero, and at least their value of fighting to the end;
  • it is at most the prize times their own estimate of their chance of winning the war; and
  • it never rises as the machine holds more forts, as the first number in the humans’ updated belief rises, holding the second number, the fort state and the date fixed. The first number starts at its initial setting and increases with each machine win, and the second does the same for human wins. The humans’ expected value also never rises, or as the humans’ cost per battle rises.

The part about the machine’s forts is checked by the program for fixed beliefs. For a fixed date, it is proved on paper only. When the humans make the offers instead, the stopping-value rules from Part 5 hold with the two sides’ roles swapped.

I count each war as ending in settlement, surrender or decisive victory

Following the 2004 model, I count every war as ending in one of three ways:

  • settlement at a positive offer: the answering side accepts a share above zero;
  • surrender: the answering side accepts exactly zero (the humans when the machine makes the offers, the machine when the humans do);
  • decisive victory: one side takes every fort.

Total settlement is the first two together. A near-zero deal, such as the humans’ share of 0.11 of 30 at a human cost of 3, counts as settlement, not surrender.

One ratio marks the crossing, in this baseline only

To compare human costs, I use one ratio. It is the humans’ expected cost of fighting to the end, as a share of the prize value they expect to win, both measured at the start. In the baseline this ratio is about 0.574 times their cost per battle. The crossing moves with the battle odds, the beliefs and the number of forts, so the ratio marks it only in this baseline.

The 2004 article leaves the true battle odds unspecified in its example. So the baseline runs set them at even, and the machine’s cost advantage works alone.

With a free machine at even odds, settlement crosses one half between human costs of 0.35 and 0.40

With a free machine and even odds, total settlement rises past one half of all wars somewhere between a human cost of 0.35 and 0.40 per battle. In the ratio above, that is between 0.20 and 0.23. Across that step, settlement rises from 0.414 to 0.506 when the machine makes the offers, and from 0.381 to 0.515 when the humans do (Figure 5).

Computed outcomes with a free machine at even battle odds (certified decisions). Each cell gives the case where the machine makes the offers, then the case where the humans do. Chances are per war.

When the machine makes the offers, much of the settlement is surrender

With the machine making the offers, surrender is 0.227 of all wars at a human cost of 0.5 and 0.289 at 0.75. So settlement at a positive offer is only 0.431 and 0.452 of all wars, below half. On the full grid, settlements that leave the humans at least 0.05 of the prize are likeliest at a human cost of 1.50, at 0.280 of all wars. Total settlement there is 0.874, and 0.594 of wars settle with the humans getting less than that.

With the humans making the offers and a free machine, surrender never happens, at any human cost. The reason is built into the model. The machine’s value of refusing is at least the prize times its own estimate of winning the war, which is above zero. In the baseline with a free machine at even odds, under the selected tie rule, I prove that for a human cost of 2.5 or more, total settlement exceeds one half whichever side makes the offers.

Who offers, and whether the machine fights for free, both move the terms a lot

The terms differ greatly even with the side making the offers held fixed. At a human cost of 1 with the machine making the offers, the humans’ share given settlement is 8.83 of 30 when both sides pay the same cost, but 2.11 when the machine fights for free.

Above the crossing, with a free machine making the offers, the humans keep an average of 2.71 of 30 among wars that settle at a cost of 0.4. That average is between 1.86 and 2.35 for costs from 0.5 to 2. When the humans make the offers, their average share among wars that settle is 6.16 to 9.90 across costs from 0.1 to 4. At a cost of 3 with machine offers, every war settles, and the humans’ share is always below 0.05 of the prize.

With the machine making the offers, the humans surrender at the outset only above a human cost of about 3.030 (a ratio of about 1.739). The published rule would put that line at a cost above 1.742 (a ratio of 1). There the humans’ value of fighting to the end at the start is zero, but their value of refusing is still 5.98.

Below the crossing, most wars are fought to a decision

For human costs of 0.35 and below, decisive victory ends more than half of wars. With the machine making the offers, it ends 0.718, 0.895 and 0.995 of wars at costs of 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1.

At even odds, a war fought to the end from the middle of the ten-fort baseline lasts 25 battles on average. The deadline already exceeds that at costs of 0.4 and 0.5, at 39 and 32. It lengthens to 48, 68 and 127 as the cost falls to 0.3, 0.2 and 0.1. Settlements that do come in play come late, after 32.0, 52.2 and 112.1 battles on average.

Three cautions apply to this crossing

  1. That the crossing at even odds lies between human costs of 0.35 and 0.40 is a computed property of this baseline. It is not a general boundary given by a formula.
  2. The humans’ cost per battle, which governs the crossing, is not measured here, and the historical record measures such costs badly. Of the costs in Bueno de Mesquita and Lalman’s (1992) game, Signorino judged such data “difficult, if not impossible, to obtain” (Signorino 1999).
  3. Both sides in the model learn at the same rate from public battles. Lopsided learning lies outside the model. An example is the bombing that, as Smith and I wrote, “probably shifted Serb beliefs to a far greater extent than those of NATO” (Smith and Stam 2004).

Part 7. Who is right, how far apart beliefs start, and how long the war runs all change how often wars settle

Who is right changes the chance of settlement a great deal

Plans depend only on the starting beliefs and the battles seen. But how often a war settles before one side loses every fort depends on the true battle odds. I compare three, with a free machine. In the first, the machine wins one battle in three, so the humans’ starting average is right. In the second, the odds are even. In the third, the machine wins two in three, so the machine’s starting average is right (Figure 6).

  • At a human cost of 1, with the machine making the offers, settlement before a decisive victory has a chance of 0.327 if the humans are right, 0.789 at even odds, and 0.979 if the machine is right. With the humans making the offers, the chances are 0.592, 0.891 and 0.987.
  • At a human cost of 0.5, the chances are 0.116, 0.658 and 0.972 with machine offers, and 0.184, 0.686 and 0.843 with human offers.
  • When the humans are right and the machine makes the offers, settlement becomes likelier than not only above a human cost that lies between 1.30 and 1.35, on a finer grid. At 1.30, settlement is 0.458, so a decisive victory ends most wars.

In these runs, beliefs further apart give later deadlines and less settlement

Next I vary the starting beliefs, holding a free machine, a human cost of 0.5, a prize of 30 and even odds. In the baseline, the deadlines are 32 with machine offers and 25 with human offers. Settlement is 0.658, with 0.227 surrender, and 0.686, with none. The humans’ shares given settlement are 2.19 and 6.62.

  • Beliefs further apart (six and two for the machine, two and six for the humans): deadlines of 73 and 55, settlement of 0.289 and 0.272 with no surrender, and human shares of 1.19 and 3.26.
  • Beliefs closer together (three and two, against two and three): deadlines of 15 and 12, settlement of 0.854 and 0.969 with no surrender, and human shares of 6.86 and 12.41.

Across every pair of beliefs, a positive human cost keeps the chance of settlement above zero. I prove this in general, under the selected tie rule. Take any beliefs of the model’s kind and a war of at least three forts starting from an undecided state, with costs that add up to more than zero. Then settlement has a positive chance for every true battle odds strictly between zero and one.

In my runs, the short war rarely settles and the long war always does

Changing the number of forts also moves the outcomes. No equal-cost comparison is printed for these runs.

  • A short war of six forts, starting at state 3 and lasting about 9 battles: deadlines of 43 and 39, and settlement of only 0.012 whichever side makes the offers, with no surrender. The human shares are 5.07 and 5.62.
  • A long war of 40 forts, starting at state 20: settlement is 1.000 whichever side makes the offers. With machine offers (deadline 18), it comes after 5.8 battles on average, with 0.641 surrender and a human share of 0.94 of 30. With human offers (deadline 16), it comes after 11.7 battles, with no surrender and a human share of 10.40.

In these computed runs, beliefs further apart and shorter wars push the one-half crossing toward higher human costs. Longer wars push it toward lower ones. I have no analytical reason for the shift with war length. Using the humans’ baseline belief, I prove that their expected number of battles in a fight to the end grows more slowly than the square of the number of forts. The ratio tends to zero as the number of forts grows through even numbers, with the war starting in the middle.

Taking turns at offering still gives a finite deadline

Finally, I solve the web appendix’s version in which the sides take turns. The machine offers in even periods from the start, and the humans in odd ones. Both sides’ offering periods face the same threshold set by the sum of the costs.

When the costs add up to more than zero, I prove that the rule for working back in the game without a cut-off has exactly one solution with values between zero and the prize, and that this solution has a finite deadline. That solution gives the values of a pattern of best play that depends only on the current state and date. When both costs are positive, it covers every such pattern. Whether those values are unique when the machine fights for free and the humans pay a positive cost is open.

I also compute the web appendix’s own set-up. There both sides update their beliefs until period 400, and even odds are common knowledge from then on. With a free machine and even odds, the last battle comes in period 15 at a human cost of 1. The chance of settlement is 0.827, and the humans keep 4.14 of 30 given settlement. At a cost of 0.5, the last battle comes in period 28, settlement is 0.672, and the humans keep 3.55. These figures are not certified for the game without the period-400 cut-off. Comparisons with a later cut-off and with the recursion serve as a check on their stability.

Part 8. Against a much stronger machine, my computed wars end early, usually in surrender or outright defeat

In my runs, the strong machine’s wars end within a few battles

Suppose the machine not only fights for free, against a human cost of 0.5 per battle, but actually wins 80, 90, 95 or 99 percent of battles. Figure 7 reports the runs across the three belief pairs, with one side making every offer.

Plans depend only on beliefs and the battles seen. So raising the true odds leaves the deadline unchanged in every case, at between 12 and 73 periods. Yet the war ends long before the deadline, in about 3 to 8 battles on average. In all three belief pairs, the machine’s starting average (two in three, three in five or three in four) lies below its true chance of winning.

In these runs, negotiated settlement usually either collapses into human surrender or gives way to the machine’s decisive victory. There are two exceptions:

  • Beliefs closer together: settlement is 0.999 or higher without surrender. The humans’ share given settlement is 0.50 of 30 at 80 percent and 0.27 at 90 percent with machine offers, and 1.74 and 0.88 with human offers. It is smaller still at 95 and 99 percent.
  • Baseline beliefs at 80 percent, with human offers: settlement is 0.671 without surrender, and the humans’ share given settlement is 0.61 of 30.

Elsewhere, outcomes are harsher:

  • Baseline beliefs, machine offers: surrender is 0.899 of all wars at 80 percent and 1.000 at 99 percent.
  • Baseline beliefs, human offers: settlement falls from 0.671 at 80 percent (0.409 at 90) to 0.049 at 99 percent, as the machine’s decisive victory takes its place.
  • Beliefs further apart: five straight machine wins take every fort before the simple bargaining range opens. The machine wins decisively in 0.983 to 1.000 of wars. At 99 percent, settlement has a chance of 4.3 in a trillion with machine offers and 1.5 in ten trillion with human offers.

In the first variant, the machine’s odds rise with its lead

This part examines two variants. In the first, the machine’s chance of winning the next battle rises with its lead, at a steepness both sides know. Each side holds a belief about the machine’s chance at the starting state. Exact updating then depends on the whole path of battles, so I solve it with bounds. I run 72 cases with rising odds at a human cost of 0.5 and 24 at a cost of 1, beside the fixed-odds cases. Each result is an interval. It bounds the result for a game whose cut-off is period 309 or later. Play is worked out to a fixed depth (36 battles at the gentlest setting and 32 at the two steeper ones), and what can happen beyond that depth is bounded. The lower bound also subtracts an allowance for the rule applied at the cut-off date.

  • At a human cost of 0.5 and the steepest setting tried, total settlement lies between 0.999 and 1.000. Surrender and human shares vary by case.
  • With beliefs further apart, at a human cost of 0.5 and the two gentler settings, the machine’s outright victory reaches the interval from 0.781 to 0.801. Total settlement falls to between 0.083 and 0.118.
  • Under baseline beliefs, with a free machine, a human cost of 0.5, the gentlest setting and an even chance at the start, the humans’ outright victory spans 0.347 to 0.371 across the two offering sides.

For the surrender and share intervals, the allowance for error from numerically averaging over beliefs is estimated from computations. No date by which fighting must stop is established for this variant.

In the second variant, under the humans’ baseline belief, an accurate and firmly held machine belief makes settlement near-certain in the cases run

In the second variant, the machine’s starting average is moved to its true chance, 0.8 or 0.9. I measure how firmly a starting belief is held by adding its two numbers, a measure I call precision in the technical paper. The baseline has a precision of 6, and the variant also tries 10 and 20. Against the humans’ baseline belief, with a free machine, centring at the original firmness of 6 leaves settlement with human offers at 0.671 and 0.409. So correcting the machine’s average alone leaves the decline in settlement intact.

With the humans making the offers, raising the firmness from 6 to 10 or 20 at the centred average changes their decision at state 9 in period 4. After four straight machine wins, one fort from defeat, they switch from fighting to settling. Total settlement under the humans’ baseline belief rises to 0.999 and 1.000. Why a firmer machine belief moves that decision is not derived.

At a firmness of 10, with a free machine and a human cost of 0.5, the computed results (with certified decisions) are:

  • Humans’ baseline belief: nearly every war settles whichever side makes the offers (0.999 at 80 percent, 1.000 at 90). With machine offers, it is almost all surrender (0.993 and 1.000 of wars). With human offers, the humans keep 0.07 and 0.01 of 30 given settlement.
  • Humans’ belief of two and three: settlement is again 0.999 and 1.000. Under machine offers it is mostly surrender (0.900 and 0.999 of wars).
  • Humans’ belief of two and six: settlement nearly vanishes (0.005 and 0.003 at 80 percent, 0.000 at 90). The machine wins decisively in 0.994 to 1.000 of wars.

Raising the firmness at the centred average also lengthens every deadline reported for this variant. With a free machine, it lowers settlement further under the humans’ belief of two and six. At 80 percent, settlement (with machine offers and with human offers) falls from 0.009 and 0.005 when the machine’s firmness is 8, matching that human belief’s firmness, to 0.005 and 0.003 at 10, and to 0.002 and 0.001 at 20. By contrast, in the cases run under the humans’ baseline belief, a firmer machine belief makes settlement near-certain, with the humans keeping at most 0.07 of 30.

Part 9. What is proved, what is computed, and what I do not claim

I keep apart what the model proves and what I show only for particular numbers. The technical paper’s appendix records which claims in Sections B.9 through B.11 and in the summary table are proved and which are computed.

What is proved and checked by the program

The formal results listed in the technical paper’s ledger are proved and checked in Lean 4. They rest on twelve files, none of which leaves a proof unfinished. None of the project’s 2,995 theorems relies on a basic assumption beyond the program’s standard three. The program checks that a proof establishes its formal statement, not that the statement matches the English. So each theorem was read against its English claim in separate blind readings.

Proved and checked by the program:

  • The corrected rule. Under best play, offers worth more than refusing are accepted and offers worth less are refused. The value of refusing is at least the value of fighting to the end.
  • The 2004 results, amended. Proposition 1 holds and sharpens. Lemma 1’s convergence of beliefs holds. Propositions 2 and 3 hold in amended form when the prize is worth something, or when the machine’s cost is zero and it makes the offers. Proposition 2 also needs the model’s kind of beliefs and costs that add up to more than zero.
  • The failures of the published rule. It fails on printed Figure 3 at state 6 in period 5, given the cells as transcribed. It fails whenever the value of fighting to the end is zero or more at a settlement state and below zero at a later one the war can reach through fighting. And it fails at every late date in the article’s example.
  • Best play and uniqueness. The plan built from stopping values is best play whatever the costs. Values, offers and clear choices are the same in every pattern of best play when the prize is worth something, or when the machine’s cost is zero and it makes the offers. At a prize of zero, with a machine cost of 1 and a human cost of 0, two patterns of best play give the machine minus 1 and 0. When the humans make the offers, the rules that build best play from stopping values swap the two sides’ roles.
  • The error from a finite horizon. Working back from a finite end date makes an error no larger than the chance that the war outlasts that date. Given three computed numbers, this certifies every choice in the equal-cost baseline at a cost of 1.
  • The deadline. Where the answering side’s value of refusing is zero or more, the offering side prefers settling now to fighting once and settling next period exactly when its gain from waiting is at most the sum of the costs. For the model’s kind of beliefs, a prize worth something, and costs that add up to more than zero, every pattern of best play settles by a finite deadline (unless the war is decided first) whose bound grows in proportion to the prize divided by the sum of the costs. So the humans’ cost alone keeps the deadline finite with a free machine. For the baseline beliefs with machine offers, the deadline also has a lower bound of the same kind, for small enough costs. As the machine’s cost rises, the states where it strictly prefers to fight shrink, and the computed plan’s deadline never moves later when it is finite.
  • The simple bargaining range. Proposition 1’s condition is needed for any settlement and, for the model’s kind of beliefs, opens eventually whenever the humans’ cost is above zero.
  • The humans’ value under machine offers: the floor, ceiling and directions set out in Part 6, except that the fixed-date part for the machine’s forts is proved on paper only.
  • Settlement chances. Under the selected tie rule, settlement is likelier than not in the baseline with a free machine at even odds for every human cost of 2.5 or more, whichever side offers, and has a positive chance for any beliefs of the model’s kind, in a war of at least three forts from an undecided starting state, when the costs add up to more than zero and the odds lie strictly between zero and one. Under the humans’ baseline belief, their expected number of battles in a fight to the end grows more slowly than the square of the number of forts, along even fort counts with the start in the middle.
  • Taking turns. With turn-taking in the game without a cut-off, when the costs add up to more than zero, the recursion has exactly one solution with values between zero and the prize. That solution has a finite deadline and gives the values of best play that depends only on the current state and date.

Proved on paper only, not checked by the program

  • the rule at an exact tie between an offer and the value of refusing;
  • that the humans’ value does not rise with the machine’s forts at a fixed date;
  • the one-step test behind the floors of 80 and 278 on the last battle;
  • that the formal requirement on best play rules out no plan.

What does “best play” require in the formal proofs? In the formal proofs, best play is a plan whose expected payoffs exist and which no change with existing expected payoffs improves on. That clause is a technical requirement of the formal setting. It excludes no plan, because a random walk along a finite line of forts reaches an end in finite expected time. At even odds, from state 5 of 10, that takes 25 battles on average. Under any plan, the number of battles fought is bounded by the length of a fight to the end. The expected length of that fight stays bounded across all battle odds, so averaging over either side’s beliefs still gives finite expected payoffs. That this requirement excludes no plan is proved on paper, not checked by the program.

Three patterns held in every computed baseline case and still failed

Formalizing the model also refuted three guesses that every computed baseline case had supported:

  1. that the corrected rule’s deadline is never later than the published rule’s;
  2. that the humans’ value falls with time, at the same fort state and the same average belief;
  3. that the last battle never moves later as the humans’ cost rises.

All three hold in a two-fort war, where every battle is decisive, and across the computed baseline cases. But each fails in a counterexample, checked by the program, in a war of three forts. In the first, the published rule settles at the start while the corrected rule fights a battle first. In the second, the humans’ value is higher in period 2 than at the start, at the same state and an average belief of one half. In the third, with a prize of 10, raising the humans’ cost from 1.5 to 2.5 moves the last battle from period 0 to period 1.

What is still open

  • Whether taking turns gives the same values in every pattern of best play when both costs are positive, not only in patterns that depend on the current state and date. This is argued, not proved.
  • Whether, with turn-taking, the values of best play that depends only on the current state and date are unique when the machine’s cost is zero and the humans’ cost is above zero.
  • A date by which fighting must stop in the variant where the machine’s odds rise with its lead, under exact updating.
  • Any general limit on the humans’ share as the machine grows stronger, beyond what works through the humans’ own beliefs.

What is only computed

The specific deadlines, settlement chances and shares are computed. For the fixed-odds cases under the text’s definitions, a second calculation starts beyond the proved deadline for every pattern of best play and certifies the choices against explicit bounds on error from the cut-off and from arithmetic. The two-departure reproduction of the printed tables has no such certificate. The variant in which odds rise with the lead uses bounds at a finite depth. A second program produced compatible, wider intervals, and the allowance for error from numerically averaging over beliefs remains an estimate from computations.

What I do not model, have not measured, and do not claim

My contribution is the correction of the 2004 rule and the extension of the 2004 model to unequal costs per battle. The numbers are one baseline with sensitivity runs. They are not a general proof of shares or of how long wars last.

The model leaves out:

  • lopsided learning, where one side learns more from a battle than the other;
  • choices made with error;
  • true battle odds that arise inside the model. The 2004 article leaves the odds unspecified in its example, and I set them at seven fixed values across Parts 6 to 8.

Most important, in every random-walk forts model the loser survives because the model is built that way. Reaching either end of the line ends the game, and there is no move that removes the other player. That is an assumption of the model, not a finding about survival. The War Baseline takes this up.

I have not measured the humans’ cost per battle. The crossing between human costs of 0.35 and 0.40 is a result for the baseline at even odds. How the 2004 article first computed its printed Figures 1 and 3 remains unresolved by the two departures that reproduce them. And no published figure confirms the unequal-cost computations reported here.

How these models bear on power transition theory and the commitment problem belongs to The War Baseline. How the traditions that assume shared or differing starting beliefs weigh on the AI transition belongs to Disagreement Without Hidden Information.

What would change the answer

Within the model, the computed answers move with the numbers chosen. The crossing moves with the true odds, the starting beliefs and the number of forts. Who is right moves the chance of settlement a great deal (Part 7). With the humans’ baseline belief and the humans making the offers, a firmer machine belief at the centred average switches the humans to settling one fort from defeat and makes settlement near-certain in the cases run (Part 8). And three patterns that held in every computed baseline case failed in a three-fort war, so a pattern seen in my runs is not thereby a law of the model. Beyond the model, what lopsided learning, choices made with error, or a side able to remove the other would do is not modelled here.

Part 10. A corrected model, a deadline that survives free fighting, and a loser who survives by assumption

Three conclusions follow for a reader of The War Baseline and Disagreement Without Hidden Information.

  1. Most of what the earlier random-walk and spiral models supply is argument or worked example, for a cost both sides share. Solving the 2004 model for best play requires replacing its published rule with the answering side’s true value of refusing.
  2. In my extension to unequal costs, settlement by learning still comes by a finite deadline if the sides hold the model’s kind of beliefs, the prize is worth something, and the two costs add up to more than zero, unless the war is decided first. Because the offering side bears both sides’ costs of delay, a positive human cost alone bounds the deadline. In the computed baseline, decisive victory often comes first when costs are small: with chance 0.995 for a free machine at a human cost of 0.1 and even odds. With a free machine at even odds, total settlement passes half of all wars once the humans’ cost passes a point between 0.35 and 0.40, but with machine offers much of it is surrender. In my runs with a free machine and a human cost of 0.5, when the machine wins four battles in five or more and its starting average lies below its true chance, wars usually end in decisive victory or surrender, except when beliefs start close together or at 80 percent with human offers in the baseline.
  3. In all of these models the loser survives because the game has no move that removes the other player. In The War Baseline I consider what happens when a stronger actor cannot credibly promise to leave a weaker rival in place. In Disagreement Without Hidden Information I compare bargaining without hidden information to bargaining in which sides start with shared beliefs and try to learn each other’s private information, before one side becomes dominant.

Where to read more

  • Fighting for Free, the technical paper: the formal set-up of the corrected and extended 2004 model, the proofs, the ledger of what the program checks, and the full tables of computed results.
  • The War Baseline, another paper of this series: it draws on these models. I take from it the margin of error on the arms-race estimate and the treatment of the commitment problem outside the forts model.
  • Disagreement Without Hidden Information, another paper of this series: it draws on these models and on Smith’s 1998 draft. I leave to it how the shared-belief and differing-belief traditions weigh on the AI transition.

Full references for the works cited as (Name Year) are in the technical paper.

The technical paper: Allan C. Stam, “Fighting for Free,” posted at https://updates.tacklebx.com/read/fighting-for-free-technical.pdf. It holds the models, proofs and sources behind this guide, and its Declarations name the source checks still open.

Proof status: A Lean build reports no unfinished proofs in the twelve modules the results rest on and no axioms beyond Lean’s three standard ones, and a script found no problems in 78 theorem names. Finding a name shows that a theorem exists, not what it assumes, and the comparison of Result 1 with its Lean statements covers an earlier wording.

AI assistance: AI models did much of the work, under my direction. I posed the paper’s questions, proposed its main arguments and models, ruled on its scope, structure and claims, and corrected drafts. Claude models planned the paper, checked its mathematics and facts, drew the figures and read most of the cited works. Gemini models checked the plan, drafted and repaired the text, and judged reported source problems. The safeguards included the Lean proofs and the name check, a second model family’s review of source problems, two reviews per review round, and computational reruns, though some second-family recomputations remain unconfirmed.
